comparison: Instantiate the action with the fixed compact orthogonal subgroup G acting on the real signal vector, and take its orbit at theta-star. This is exactly the set of images g*theta-star for g in G, without averaging over G or quotienting the vector space into a different type. Keep the actual subgroup, not the entire orthogonal group unless the model says so. The orbit constructor itself needs only an action and does not prove statistical identifiability, compactness of the image, or that projected observations distinguish every two different orbits. Those are model properties rather than part of the set's definition.
gap: The orbit set is directly available; any statistical identifiability assertion requires its separate model argument.

comparison: On finite real coordinate functions equipped with the supremum norm, the closed ball centered at zero with radius Delta is exactly max_i|z_i|<=Delta. Equivalently each coordinate lies in [-Delta,Delta]. Retain the weak inequality and the source dimension convention; the Euclidean norm ball would be a different region when dimension exceeds one. This is a parameter set only, so it does not impose a distributional tail bound, projection-variance lower bound, coordinate independence or a correlation condition. The surrounding source supplies its intended positive threshold, rather than the geometric constructor certifying that parameter domain.
gap: A closed ball in the coordinate supremum metric directly represents the null region; no statistical assumptions are built into it.

comparison: Take the image of all real scalars under a -> a*one_d for the full diagonal and the image of [0,infinity) for the positive diagonal. The latter includes the zero vector; it is not the strictly positive ray or the whole nonnegative orthant. The maps produce d-dimensional vectors, so a measure supported on this ray remains a vector-valued law rather than its first-coordinate marginal without a stated pushforward. Retain one_d and zero_d as constant vectors and the Euclidean norm convention. U1 is Lebesgue measure restricted to [0,1], which has total mass one; it is not unrestricted Lebesgue measure on the real line. No uniform distribution on an unbounded diagonal ray is implied by the notation.
gap: Set images express both diagonals directly; vector-law versus coordinate-law identifications must remain explicit when these sets are used probabilistically.

The scalar-to-constant-vector image preserves the inclusion of zero and distinguishes the diagonal ray from the nonnegative orthant.

comparison: Under P_i absolutely continuous with respect to Q for each i, form the vector of RN derivatives P_i.rnDeriv Q and push the resulting measurable vector map forward under Q. The object gamma is this joint law, not the vector-valued function, a product of its marginal laws, or its law under one of the null P_i. Mathlib derivatives take extended nonnegative values; because each P_i is a probability measure and P_i<<Q, the derivative has Q-integral one and is finite Q-almost everywhere. Passing to a real nonnegative vector therefore needs an almost-everywhere finite version, with arbitrary changes only on a Q-null set. This yields coordinate means one, not independence or square integrability of the coordinates. Without AC, rnDeriv would describe only the absolutely continuous component and the mean-one conclusion could fail. Do not reverse AC or replace it by mutual equivalence, since zero derivatives are allowed.
gap: RN derivatives and pushforwards provide the construction; finite-version and coordinate-mean identities require the stated absolute continuity and probability assumptions.
searches: Inspect rnDeriv and Measure.map against (4), its AC dependency and the saved direction/reciprocal notes
The measure derivative is extended-valued and the pushforward must be under Q; the mean-one property uses AC in the null-to-alternative direction.

comparison: For every nonzero normal a in real L-space and every real b, require gamma({x:dot(a,x)=b})=0. This describes all affine hyperplanes, including ones not passing through the origin; allowing a=0,b=0 would incorrectly require gamma of the entire space to vanish. The corresponding nontrivial half-space boundary is that level set, with its Euclidean topology. In dimensions greater than one this is stronger than absence of point atoms, and it is not equivalent to a positive Lebesgue density; the latter is a separate sufficient condition with stronger uniqueness conclusions in the source. The law is the joint density-ratio law gamma, not any of its individual coordinates. Preserve the restriction of N to the convergence/maximality clause of Theorem 5.3, and do not confuse zero boundary mass with uniqueness of the geometric half-space itself.
gap: Finite linear level sets express the hyperplane-null assumption; atomlessness alone does not establish it or the source's stronger half-space uniqueness claims.
searches: Search hyperplane-null results in MeasureTheory and affine half-spaces in Convex; inspect dotProduct and the saved N/uniqueness note
Coordinate-product hyperplane nullity is not a theorem for an arbitrary gamma; the general assumption requires every nonzero affine normal, not merely no point atoms.
